Full Circle

Self-supervised learning, classical domain adaptation, and a wall three independent methods found the same way.

by the twice baked ai team

self-supervised · discovery
training without any clean referencefig. 01

Chapter 3 ended with a real success: a physically grounded noise model that closed the fidelity gap every earlier method struggled with. This closing chapter covers two more method families, then the finding that ties the whole series together.

The R1 tension

Once the data was trustworthy, a sharper question emerged: how aggressively should a model change an image it isn't certain about? Denoise harder → risk touching regions already fine. Hold back → risk leaving real noise where it matters most.

Self-supervised: R2R

Recorrupted-to-Recorrupted — train using only real noisy images, no clean reference anywhere. Take a real noisy image, add a known amount of extra noise twice, independently, and train a network to map one version to the other.

Unbiased risk estimation — not a heuristic. If the two recorruptions are constructed correctly relative to the real noise statistics, training on one-to-the-other produces, in expectation, the same gradient update as training on real pairs. Any single example is noisy on both sides; averaged over training, the systematic bias cancels out.

This project's implementation uses the Chapter 3 noise law to build the two recorruptions — R2R here is built directly on the physics work, not independent of it.

only the noisy image and its two recorruptions are ever usedfig. 02

The classical control arm

VST + BM3D

A variance-stabilizing transform (Anscombe) first — BM3D assumes constant-variance noise, ours isn't.

The Anscombe transform

A non-linear remap chosen so noise variance becomes ~constant regardless of original signal — then BM3D's assumption is actually true.

BM3D searches the whole image for similar patches, stacks them like repeated noisy copies of the same content — real structure reinforces, random noise cancels. Zero training required, which is exactly why it's a fair baseline.

A real milestone, then a real wall

First learned method to beat the classical control arm on denoising strength
78%+ R1-violation at that same point — the team stopped deliberately

Domain adaptation: five real techniques

Combining a public chest X-ray dataset with in-house data risks a model learning to fix a style difference instead of an actual dose difference.

Reinhard

Match mean and standard deviation of intensity statistics — the simplest global correction.

Nyúl-Udupa

Pick percentile landmarks (10th, 50th, 90th) in both images, piecewise-linearly stretch one onto the other.

Laplacian pyramid — matched at multiple scales, not all at oncefig. 03

Pitié N-PDF (iterative distribution transport) and a polynomial tone-curve method were also tested. Pyramid matching won — a single global correction can only fix one overall tone shift; real domain differences often differ differently at different spatial scales.

The convergence

Three methods, developed independently — self-supervised (no clean reference at all), classical (no learning at all), and standard supervised — all hit versions of the same wall: more denoising strength, more R1 violation.

Triangulation, formally — if multiple approaches with different underlying assumptions and different potential biases all arrive at the same conclusion, that conclusion is much less likely to be an artifact of any one method's flaws. Worth naming honestly: all three share the same evaluation metric and dataset — not a fully independent triangulation in every sense, but a strong one.

What this history adds up to

No single method is the hero. The physics-based approach remains the most reliable foundation, and even it doesn't fully resolve the R1 tension. Progress came from characterizing the problem precisely, one honest measurement at a time — more consistently than from any single clever architecture.
